title: Australia Regulates Supplements Like Drugs, but Nobody Checks Whether They Work
dek: Australia puts supplements and pharmaceuticals under the same agency, which looks strict; but efficacy is neither reviewed before market nor tested during production — the impression of "good" was planted by marketing and cross-border policy.
why: The first half's regulatory breakdown is solid, and the back half's chain from marketing to daigou policy is complete; but the middle section has a lot of transcription garbage, so the information density is uneven.
who: Investors and founders looking at consumer brands, supplements and cross-border e-commerce, plus anyone doing brand marketing or interested in where regulatory arbitrage exists.

points.h: Australians taking pills is a tradition, not a climate
points.body: The soil for Australia's supplement industry isn't the natural environment, it's four social habits: a sparse population that encourages self-medication, pharmacists who also diagnose and dispense, a naturopathy industry body dating to the 1920s, and health food stores resembling food-as-medicine shops. Stacked together, these four made Australians used to "solving health problems without going to the hospital." Black Moth (澳佳宝) started as a naturopathy clinic; only after the second generation took over did it translate that into products the mainstream system could recognise — turning "take a spoonful of fish oil a day" into standardised fish oil capsules.

points.h: The contract manufacturers are the industry's foundation
points.body: Pen Pharmaceuticals, which appeared in 1974, was Australia's first company focused on contract manufacturing of supplements, and by around 2003 it was producing roughly 70% of Australia's vitamins, minerals and herbal products. Its value lay in process know-how: tablets, compound ingredients, the oil-and-gelatin seal of soft capsules, the mixing uniformity of powders, the stability of liquids — each is its own set of solutions. In the 1980s and 90s a new generation of contract manufacturers extended service in both directions, moving from pure production (CMO) to CDMO covering formulation, ingredients, trial production, labelling, packaging, testing, and registration for export. The brand only has to hand over a concept, and the factory can turn it into a product ready to sell.

points.h: Registration means nobody looks before it hits the shelf
points.body: Australia legislated in 1989, putting the TGA in charge of both pharmaceuticals and supplements, and all products must obtain an AUST number. Most supplements fall into the AUSTL category: only low-risk ingredients permitted by the TGA, only low-level health claims, and companies get a number just by applying themselves — the TGA does no pre-market review, only post-market spot checks. By around 2010 Australia had roughly ten thousand complementary medicines, of which nearly 98% were in this registration system. Only prescription drugs, over-the-counter drugs and a small number of high-risk supplements enter the AUSTR tier, which requires the TGA to assess safety, quality and efficacy in advance.

points.h: It looks strict, but in practice it is loose
points.body: Put contract manufacturing and regulation together and you see that GMP only guarantees the factory produces consistently to the standard the brand gives it, and that problems can be traced to a batch recall — it is not itself responsible for whether the product works. The TGA side only handles declarations and issuing batch numbers; efficacy is explained by the brand itself. So the claim that "Australia regulates supplements like drugs" is not wrong, but it is misleading: the method of control is the same, but the degree of control over the efficacy part differs enormously. The whole system does no effective upfront oversight of a product's actual effect, and there is a risk of disconnect between the brand and the product's efficacy.

points.h: The marketing was copied from Centrum, not invented
points.body: CEO Radek Sali, who took over in 2008, did not conjure a marketing plan out of thin air. He did industry research and found that the best-selling peer was Centrum, and feedback from retailers was: Centrum didn't give the channel much profit, but it was on TV all year round with heavy advertising and good athlete endorsements, and consumers would ask for it by name when they walked into a pharmacy. Sali wanted to replicate this at Swisse. He first invested in Australia's national sport, cricket — the men's team captain, buying only very short ad slots during the hottest summer cricket broadcasts, so that even a limited budget could appear at important moments. But the female-dominated sales channel wasn't impressed; one buyer didn't watch cricket herself and didn't know the athlete. He asked his mother what shows she liked, and she said a dance variety show, and the strategy pivoted to spoken-word placements in entertainment content.

Swisse's bigger promotional push drew on Oprah and Ellen, and signed actress Nicole Kidman for three years, extending its reach from Australia to the US. By 2012 Swisse had 25 brand ambassadors, had shot more than 80 TV commercials in the previous 12 months, and reached annual revenue of 183 million Australian dollars, with marketing spend of 40 to 50 million Australian dollars a year — reportedly at one point the highest marketing spend of any consumer brand in Australia. Its ads didn't emphasise efficacy or ingredients; they mainly presented a state of being energetic, self-disciplined and good-looking — turning health into a lifestyle consumers aspire to. In 2012 Swisse took more than 20% market share in Australian supermarkets and more than 10% in pharmacies.

points.h: The growth engine was found in Chinese pharmacies
points.body: Swisse's expensive push into the US market wasn't a success, and on returning to Australia it found that Swisse sold extremely well in pharmacies in Chinese-populated areas — some stores sold at ten times the level of ordinary stores — because students and Chinese immigrants bought in bulk to take back to China or resell online, i.e. daigou. Two policy shifts came in 2015: in March the Hangzhou cross-border e-commerce comprehensive pilot zone was approved, and in June China and Australia signed a free trade agreement, which took effect in December that year. The FTA mainly affected ordinary trade; Australian official statistics put the tariff on vitamins and supplements generally at 3% to 10%, while Black Moth itself estimated an average of 20%, and after the agreement it was said the rate could fall to zero within four years. Cross-border e-commerce went through bonded warehouses, platforms bought in bulk, logistics time and cost fell sharply, and such goods were treated in policy as for personal use, so they didn't have to go through the registration and filing process for supplement imports.

points.h: The brand was bought; the impression stayed put
points.body: In September 2015, Hong Kong-listed Biostime completed the acquisition of a controlling stake in Swisse, and two years later completed a full buyout, at a deal size of about 1.7 billion Australian dollars, or 8.7 billion RMB. For Swisse the deal carried little premium; for Biostime it added a large chunk of business revenue and imagination. Now all those Swisse ads on Hunan TV variety shows are, in theory, a Chinese supplement company spending money, yet the brand can still say it is an Australian supplement brand, and consumers can still apply their old vague good impression of Australia to it — the core value of the acquisition rests, in large proportion, in brand goodwill.

An internationally common production standard that ensures consistent production to standard and traceable recalls, but is not responsible for efficacy.

quotes.text: The GMP system itself is not responsible for the product's efficacy; it can only prove that the contract manufacturer produced to the standard the brand gave it.
The whole system actually looks strict but is loose in practice, especially when it comes to the efficacy part.
This looseness means that no part of the system does any effective upfront oversight of the product's actual effect.
It doesn't emphasise efficacy or ingredients; it mainly presents a state of being energetic, self-disciplined and good-looking — turning health into a lifestyle consumers aspire to.
The supplement industry has no particular barrier to entry; if everyone doesn't compete on marketing, for now they haven't found the next thing to compete on.
When consumers face something they aren't familiar with, it's actually very easy for them to string together other familiar and trustworthy concepts to understand this unfamiliar thing.

We tend to remember very simple concepts or judgments, so simple that you forget how many layers of logic lie behind them. So the more a business idea looks like common sense, the more it's worth asking one more question: how did it come about, and how did it become so-called common sense?
